newsitem.title: FRENCH POLYNESIA: Fragile Kon-Tiki successor to cross South Pacific.
newsitem.headline: Fragile Kon-Tiki successor to cross South Pacific.

text.p: Fifty years after the Kon-Tiki raft showed that ancient peoples from South America may have sailed the oceans, a new fragile boat sets out across the South Pacific on Sunday.

A Spanish-led expedition will sail westwards from Easter Island on the Mata Rangi, a 30-metre (100 ft) long reed boat, to show that local peoples may have had links with cultures towards Asia, rather than with South America.
Kitin Munoz, the leader of the expedition, said the vessel would sail to the French archipelago of Gambier, then to Tahiti and on to New Zealand via the Cook Islands, Samoa and perhaps Fiji.

Norway's Thor Heyerdahl set out from Peru on April 27, 1947 aboard the balsa raft Kon-Tiki for an epic 101-day voyage that showed that Easter Island and other coral atolls might have been populated from South America, thousands of km (miles) to the east.

Heyerdahl, a Norwegian, reckoned there was a link between sun worship by predecessors of the Incas in Peru and religious beliefs in Easter Island, where local peoples left mysterious stone carvings of monumental elongated faces.
But most modern researchers believe the islands scattered around the Polynesian triangle -- between Easter Island, Hawaii and New Zealand -- were populated by peoples from Asia.

Calling himself the "spiritual son of Thor Heyerdahl", Munoz told a news conference in Tahiti the trip would show the Easter Islanders were not isolated from cultures to the west, even though they lacked materials for boat building.
He said the Mata Rangi was made from reeds from the crater lake of Maunga Terevaka on Easter Island and assembled by Indians who live around Lake Titicaca in the Andes.
The same Indians, who still use the techniques for their own vessels, built the Ra vessels Heyerdahl used to sail across the Atlantic.
The Mata Rangi, which weighs 70 tonnes, will set sail from the Anakena beach on the north of Easter Island. Its sails are also made of reeds and its mast of eucalyptus.
Munoz will travel with a crew of two Bolivians, one American from Hawaii, two Maoris from New Zealand, two Tahiti islanders and five or six from Easter Island, which belongs to Chile.

The crew will live off rice and local root vegetables, and fish caught during the trip. Spanish Prince Felipe, the son of King Juan Carlos who is a patron of the expedition, will travel for the first few miles of the trip.
The captain, Teiki Pambrun, reckoned that the first leg of the voyage to Gambier would take between 15 days and two months.

Mata Rangi means "Sky Eyes" in Polynesian, a contraction of the former name of Easter Island "Mata ki te Rangi". The latter means "Eyes that look at the Sky", after the mysterious stone statues with eyes of black obsidian and white coral.
